observation: Outdoor temperature normally appeared about every 7 s.
A later interval was about 17 s.
GFA P06 had previously shown occasional 1-2 minute visibility delays.
diagnosis: The upstream scheduler executes all members of a due poll group in one cycle, producing periodic latency spikes for FAST items when NORMAL/SLOW/RARE groups coincide.
The old profile had approximately 32 FAST, 21 NORMAL, 36 SLOW and 55 RARE serial transactions before byte-bit reuse.
ONCE was tied to poll_cycle==0 and upstream forcepoll/reloadpoll reset poll_cycle, so startup-only items could be replayed.
The separate P80 guard issue is fixed in GFA patch helper v1.0.3: transient P80 transport failures no longer erase a previously validated P80=20 identity.

behavior: Initial process-start cycle still seeds a complete snapshot.
Recurring groups are assigned deterministic per-transaction phases.
Completed ONCE is disabled for the remainder of the process lifetime.
forcepoll refreshes recurring groups but not completed ONCE.
Explicit forced datapoint readbacks remain unchanged.

policy: Core burner/pump/GFA process signals remain FAST.
Outdoor temperature and ordinary user setpoints move to NORMAL.
Internal BLR/CFDM values move to DIAG.
Static service/coding values and read-only weekly programs move to ONCE.
Counters and error histories remain RARE.

conclusion: The phased poll scheduler is now live on the production splitter.
The optimized VDensHO1 profile is active and Home Assistant discovery completed successfully.
The next measurement must be passive MQTT cadence observation without forcepoll, before changing olbreath.
Phased scheduling removed the previously observed 15-20 second FAST latency spikes.
All measured FAST signals, including P06/P09/P87, have a stable approximately 4.7 second median cadence at olbreath=0.15.
NORMAL group cadence is approximately 24 seconds, matching five FAST cycles.
This measurement is the baseline for controlled olbreath reduction.
100 ms olbreath passed the 180 s controlled cadence/error gate.
FAST cadence improved from about 4.7 s to about 3.5 s with no observed communication errors.
NORMAL cadence improved from about 24 s to about 17.5 s, consistent with five FAST cycles.
Proceed to a separate 50 ms test before choosing the permanent production value.

conclusion: 50 ms materially improves cadence, with FAST median near 2.13 s and NORMAL median near 10.6 s.
However, one GFA P09 read returned FF within the 180 s gate and was quarantined.
This short-run failure is sufficient to reject 50 ms as the production timing for the current hardware/software setup.
The comparison strongly suggests reduced timing margin at 50 ms, although one event alone does not prove that olbreath was the sole physical cause.
100 ms remains the fastest currently clean tested setting.

interpretation: The 100 ms short gate was insufficient to establish production stability.
A second independent GFA address (P87/0x4057) showed the same FF/timeout symptom previously seen at 50 ms on P09/0x4009.
The repeated timing-correlated FF pattern strengthens the hypothesis that reduced reply-to-next-request spacing is lowering communication margin for GFA_READ.
This does not prove olbreath is the sole cause; a long 150 ms baseline is still required to estimate the background error rate.
long_soak_olbreath_010.production_decision: Reject 0.10 as production timing pending further evidence.

rationale: Observed short-timing failures have so far occurred on direct GFA_READ 0x6B only: P09/0x4009 at global 50 ms and P87/0x4057 during the 100 ms long soak.
The existing GFA layer already recognizes a successful one-byte raw 0xFF response and quarantines it instead of publishing it as a physical value.
Ordinary F7/F4 traffic has not shown the same failure signature in the timing gates.
validation_plan: Set global olbreath to 0.05 only for the experiment.
Observe passive cadence plus first-attempt FF retry/recovery logs.
Reject on any second FF, failed retry, OL Error, restart or P80 identity failure.
If short gate passes, run a longer soak before changing the permanent profile helper.
